flashcards.front: Public vs. private vs. hybrid vs. community cloud
flashcards.back: Public: shared infrastructure owned by a third-party provider. Private: dedicated to one organization, on-premises or hosted. Hybrid: a mix of both, often connected for workload portability. Community: shared by several organizations with common requirements, like agencies in the same industry.
flashcards.detail: Exam trap: "hybrid" specifically implies connected, coordinated environments — just using two unrelated clouds for different things is closer to multi-cloud, not hybrid.

flashcards.back: Scalability is the general capacity to handle more (or less) load by adding or removing resources, which can be planned and manual. Elasticity is scaling that happens automatically and dynamically in response to real-time demand.
flashcards.detail: Every elastic system is scalable, but not every scalable system is elastic — a system that only scales through a change request ticket is scalable, not elastic.

flashcards.back: Vertical scaling ("scaling up") adds resources — CPU, RAM — to an existing instance. Horizontal scaling ("scaling out") adds more instances running in parallel.
flashcards.detail: Vertical scaling usually requires a restart and has a hardware ceiling. Horizontal scaling avoids both, but requires the workload to be designed to run across multiple instances (e.g., stateless, load-balanced).

flashcards.front: High availability vs. fault tolerance vs. disaster recovery
flashcards.back: High availability minimizes downtime through redundancy, but a brief failover interruption may still occur. Fault tolerance keeps the system running through a failure with no interruption at all, usually at higher cost. Disaster recovery is the plan and process for restoring service after a major outage that HA/fault tolerance didn't prevent.
flashcards.detail: HA and fault tolerance are about avoiding downtime; DR assumes downtime already happened and is about getting back up.

flashcards.back: RTO (Recovery Time Objective) is the maximum acceptable time to restore service after an outage. RPO (Recovery Point Objective) is the maximum acceptable amount of data loss, measured as time since the last good backup.
flashcards.detail: A 4-hour RPO means backups need to run at least every 4 hours. RTO and RPO are set by business requirements first, then the backup/DR architecture is built to meet them — not the other way around.

flashcards.front: Block vs. file vs. object storage
flashcards.back: Block storage presents raw, low-latency volumes ideal for databases and VM disks. File storage presents a shared, hierarchical filesystem accessed over a protocol like NFS or SMB. Object storage holds data as flat, metadata-rich objects, built for massive scale rather than low-latency random access.
flashcards.detail: A relational database wants block storage. A shared team drive wants file storage. Millions of backup archives or media files want object storage.

flashcards.back: Round robin cycles requests evenly across servers in order. Least connections sends new requests to whichever server currently has the fewest active connections. Weighted (round robin or least connections) accounts for servers with different capacities. Source/IP-affinity keeps a given client pinned to the same backend server.
flashcards.detail: Source affinity matters for stateful apps that keep session data on one server — losing that pinning mid-session can log a user out or break their session.

flashcards.back: Authentication verifies who you are. Authorization determines what you're allowed to do once verified. Accounting logs what was actually done, for audit purposes.
flashcards.detail: A stolen-but-valid password is an authentication success with an authorization failure waiting to happen — the identity checks out, but it isn't really that person acting.

flashcards.back: Role-based access control (RBAC) grants permissions based on a user's assigned role (e.g., "Backup Operator"). Attribute-based access control (ABAC) evaluates a combination of attributes at request time — user department, resource tag, time of day, location — to make a more granular decision.
flashcards.detail: RBAC is simpler to administer at scale; ABAC is more flexible but harder to audit because the effective rule set is computed dynamically rather than assigned directly.

flashcards.front: Encryption at rest vs. in transit vs. in use
flashcards.back: At rest protects stored data (on disk). In transit protects data moving across a network (e.g., TLS). In use protects data while it's actively being processed in memory, which is the hardest of the three to achieve and typically needs specialized hardware (e.g., a trusted execution environment).
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap: encrypting a database at rest does nothing to protect a query result being sent to a client over an unencrypted connection — that needs in-transit encryption too.

flashcards.back: A security model that never grants trust based on network location alone. Every request is independently verified — identity, device posture, and context — regardless of whether it originates inside or outside the traditional network perimeter.
flashcards.detail: Zero Trust means a compromised perimeter (e.g., a stolen VPN credential) still isn't enough on its own to reach sensitive resources, because every subsequent request is re-checked.

flashcards.back: An Intrusion Detection System (IDS) monitors traffic and alerts on suspicious activity, but doesn't block it. An Intrusion Prevention System (IPS) sits inline and can actively block or drop traffic it identifies as malicious.
flashcards.detail: IPS's ability to block traffic is also its biggest risk: a false positive can actively break legitimate traffic, which a passive IDS never would.

flashcards.back: A stateful firewall tracks the state of active connections and automatically allows return traffic for a connection it already approved. A stateless filter (like a basic ACL) evaluates every packet independently against its rule set, with no memory of prior traffic.
flashcards.detail: Stateless filtering needs explicit rules for both inbound and outbound halves of a connection, since it has no concept of "this reply belongs to a request I already allowed."

flashcards.back: Tokenization replaces sensitive data with a non-sensitive substitute (a token) that has no mathematical relationship to the original value, with the real data stored separately in a vault. Encryption transforms data using a reversible mathematical algorithm and a key.
flashcards.detail: Because a token can't be mathematically reversed back to the original value even if you had unlimited computing power, tokenization is often preferred for things like stored payment card numbers.

flashcards.back: Blue-green runs two full, identical production environments; traffic is switched entirely from one to the other once the new version is verified. Canary releases the new version to a small subset of users/traffic first, gradually increasing exposure as confidence grows.
flashcards.detail: Blue-green gives an instant, all-or-nothing rollback (just switch traffic back). Canary limits the blast radius of a bad release but takes longer to fully roll out.

flashcards.back: A rolling deployment updates instances gradually, a few at a time, so the service stays available throughout. An in-place deployment updates a server directly, typically taking that instance offline (or degraded) during the update.
flashcards.detail: Rolling deployments need a load balancer removing an instance from rotation before updating it, then adding it back — skip that step and you're serving errors from a mid-update instance.

flashcards.front: Full vs. incremental vs. differential backup
flashcards.back: A full backup copies everything. An incremental backup copies only what changed since the last backup of any kind (fastest to create, slowest to restore — needs the full plus every incremental since). A differential backup copies everything changed since the last full backup (restore needs only the full plus the latest differential).
flashcards.detail: Incremental backups are smaller and faster individually, but a restore has to replay every incremental in sequence — if one link in that chain is corrupt, the restore fails past that point.

flashcards.front: P2V, V2V, P2C, and V2C migrations
flashcards.back: P2V converts a physical server into a virtual machine. V2V moves a VM from one hypervisor/platform to another. P2C moves a still-physical on-premises workload straight into the cloud. V2C moves a workload that is already virtualized on-premises into the cloud — the distinction is what state the source was in before the move, not just where it ends up.
flashcards.detail: A 'lift and shift' cloud migration is usually a P2C or V2C migration — moving the workload largely as-is, versus refactoring it to use cloud-native PaaS services instead.

flashcards.back: Thick provisioning allocates the full requested storage capacity immediately, whether or not it's used. Thin provisioning allocates storage on demand as data is actually written, letting you over-commit total capacity across multiple volumes.
flashcards.detail: Thin provisioning's risk: if many thin-provisioned volumes are all filled close to their allocated limit at once, the underlying physical storage can run out even though each individual volume still shows free space.

flashcards.back: Defining infrastructure — networks, VMs, storage — as declarative configuration files that can be version-controlled and used to deploy the same environment repeatably, instead of manual configuration.
flashcards.detail: IaC's real value in a cert-exam sense: it makes environments idempotent and auditable — you can always tell exactly what was deployed by reading the file, and redeploying it produces the same result.

flashcards.front: Continuous integration vs. continuous delivery vs. continuous deployment
flashcards.back: Continuous integration merges code changes and runs automated tests frequently. Continuous delivery goes further, keeping code always in a releasable state after passing tests, but a human still approves the actual release. Continuous deployment removes that manual gate — every change that passes automated tests ships to production automatically.
flashcards.detail: The one-word difference between 'delivery' and 'deployment' is the whole distinction: delivery is release-ready, deployment is already released.

flashcards.back: Automation handles a single, well-defined task without human intervention (e.g., auto-restarting a failed service). Orchestration coordinates multiple automated tasks together into a larger workflow (e.g., provisioning a VM, then configuring it, then registering it with a load balancer, in sequence).
flashcards.detail: Orchestration is built ON TOP OF automation — you can't orchestrate a workflow out of steps that aren't individually automated first.

flashcards.back: Chargeback actually bills internal departments for their share of cloud costs, moving real budget between them. Showback reports each department's usage and cost for visibility and accountability, without an actual internal transfer of funds.
flashcards.detail: Showback is often adopted first, as a lower-friction way to build cost awareness before an organization is ready for the accounting complexity of real chargeback.

flashcards.back: SNMP (Simple Network Management Protocol) is used to monitor and manage network devices, polling or receiving traps about their status and metrics. Syslog is a standard for forwarding log messages from a device or application to a centralized logging server.
flashcards.detail: SNMP is generally for structured, device-health metrics (interface status, CPU load); syslog is for free-form event and log messages — the two are often run side by side, not as alternatives to each other.

flashcards.back: A baseline is the normal, expected range of a metric under typical conditions, established by observing it over time. A threshold is a specific value that, when crossed, triggers an alert or action.
flashcards.detail: Thresholds set without first establishing a baseline tend to be either too sensitive (constant false alarms) or too loose (real problems go unnoticed) — baselining comes first.

flashcards.back: A Service Level Agreement typically defines measurable commitments like uptime percentage, response time to incidents, and resolution time — along with the penalties or credits owed if those commitments aren't met.
flashcards.detail: "Five nines" (99.999% uptime) allows only about 5 minutes of downtime a year — a useful number to recognize on the exam when a scenario states an uptime percentage and asks how much downtime it allows.

flashcards.back: A centralized repository that tracks an organization's IT assets (configuration items) and the relationships between them — which servers depend on which services, who owns what, and so on.
flashcards.detail: A CMDB is what lets a change or incident process answer "what else does this affect?" instead of relying on institutional memory.

flashcards.back: A pod is the smallest deployable unit — one or more tightly-coupled containers that share networking and storage. A node is a physical or virtual machine that runs pods. A cluster is the full set of nodes managed together, coordinated by a control plane.
flashcards.detail: Scaling in Kubernetes usually means adding more pod replicas (horizontal), not making one pod bigger — matching the general cloud preference for horizontal over vertical scaling.

flashcards.back: 1) Identify the problem. 2) Establish a theory of probable cause. 3) Test the theory. 4) Establish a plan of action and implement the solution. 5) Verify full system functionality. 6) Document findings and outcomes.
flashcards.detail: A common exam trap: jumping straight to "implement a solution" without first testing the theory — a plausible-sounding cause that turns out to be wrong wastes a maintenance window and can make things worse.

flashcards.back: In a multi-tenant environment, one tenant's heavy resource usage (CPU, disk I/O, network) degrades performance for other tenants sharing the same underlying physical hardware.
flashcards.detail: The typical fix is resource governance — CPU/IO limits, quality-of-service policies, or moving the noisy workload to dedicated hardware — rather than something the affected tenant can usually fix from their own side.

flashcards.back: Cloud resources — disks, snapshots, public IPs, load balancers — left behind after the workload that created them was deleted, but never cleaned up themselves. They keep incurring cost with no one using them.
flashcards.detail: A classic root cause of 'why is our bill higher than expected' when the deployed workload footprint hasn't obviously grown.

flashcards.back: A failure where the network path and destination service are both healthy, but a hostname simply won't resolve to the correct IP address — often due to a misconfigured or stale DNS record, or a caching resolver serving an outdated answer.
flashcards.detail: A good diagnostic instinct: if a service is unreachable by name but reachable by its raw IP address, the problem is DNS, not the network path or the service itself.

flashcards.back: Latency is the delay before data begins to transfer (how long a single round trip takes). Bandwidth is the total volume of data that can transfer per unit of time once it's flowing. A connection can have plenty of bandwidth and still feel slow due to high latency.
flashcards.detail: A common trap: adding more bandwidth to a connection does nothing to fix a latency problem — they're independent characteristics with different causes and different fixes. A CDN (content delivery network) is a latency fix specifically, not a bandwidth one.

flashcards.back: A failure where infrastructure and configuration are otherwise correct, but a service stops working (or refuses to scale further) because a software license has expired or a licensed capacity limit (e.g., number of cores or seats) has been reached.
flashcards.detail: Easy to overlook because nothing about the infrastructure itself changed — the exam likes scenarios where a service 'just stopped working' with no recent configuration change, pointing at licensing or a certificate expiration instead.

flashcards.front: Root cause analysis vs. a workaround
flashcards.back: A workaround restores service quickly without necessarily fixing the underlying issue (e.g., restarting a hung service). Root cause analysis identifies and addresses the actual reason the problem happened, to prevent recurrence.
flashcards.detail: Applying a workaround isn't a mistake under time pressure — the mistake is stopping there and never following up with root cause analysis, so the same incident quietly repeats.

flashcards.back: IaaS (Infrastructure as a Service) provides raw compute, storage, and networking — the customer manages the OS upward. PaaS (Platform as a Service) adds a managed runtime/OS layer so the customer just deploys code. SaaS (Software as a Service) delivers a complete, ready-to-use application, with the provider managing everything underneath.
flashcards.detail: The customer's management responsibility shrinks as you move IaaS -> PaaS -> SaaS: with IaaS you patch the OS yourself, with SaaS you manage nothing but your own data and user accounts.

flashcards.back: A virtual machine virtualizes hardware and includes its own full guest operating system, managed by a hypervisor. A container virtualizes at the OS level, packaging an application with its dependencies but sharing the host's kernel — no separate guest OS per instance.
flashcards.detail: That shared kernel is why containers start in seconds (or less) and have a much smaller footprint than a VM, but it also means containers on the same host are less isolated from each other than separate VMs would be.

flashcards.back: MFA combines at least two of: something you know (a password or PIN), something you have (a hardware token or authenticator app), something you are (a biometric like a fingerprint), and sometimes somewhere you are (location) or something you do (behavioral).
flashcards.detail: Two passwords, or a password plus a security question, are both still just "something you know" twice — that's not true multifactor, even though it feels like an extra step.

flashcards.back: PKI issues and manages digital certificates that bind a public key to an identity, signed by a trusted Certificate Authority (CA). TLS uses this to let a client verify a server's identity and negotiate encrypted communication.
flashcards.detail: A certificate that has expired, or was issued by a CA the client doesn't trust, will fail validation even if the underlying network path and server are perfectly healthy — a common troubleshooting trap that looks like a network outage but isn't.

flashcards.back: Patch management is the process of testing, approving, and applying software/OS updates on a controlled schedule rather than ad hoc. A maintenance window is a pre-approved, communicated time slot during which changes (including patching) are allowed to cause disruption.
flashcards.detail: Testing a patch in staging before production, and scheduling the rollout in an approved window, are both change management applied specifically to patching.

flashcards.back: Using historical usage trends and baselines to forecast future resource needs (storage, compute, bandwidth) and provision ahead of demand, rather than reacting after a resource is already exhausted.
flashcards.detail: Good capacity planning depends on having a solid baseline first — without knowing normal growth trends, it's just guessing.

flashcards.front: Hot, warm, and cold DR sites
flashcards.back: A hot site is fully equipped and kept in near real-time sync with production, ready for near-instant failover (fastest, most expensive). A warm site has infrastructure in place but needs some setup/data sync before use. A cold site has only basic facilities (power, space) and needs full buildout and data restoration before use (slowest, cheapest).
flashcards.detail: Site choice is really an RTO/cost trade-off: a lower RTO requirement pushes toward a hot site, while a looser RTO can tolerate the savings of a cold site.

flashcards.back: RAID 0 stripes data across disks for performance with no redundancy (one disk failure loses everything). RAID 1 mirrors data for redundancy with no capacity gain. RAID 5 stripes data plus distributed parity, tolerating one disk failure. RAID 10 combines mirroring and striping for both redundancy and performance, at the cost of half the raw capacity.
flashcards.detail: RAID 0 is sometimes mistaken for a resilience feature because it "spreads" data across disks — it actually has zero fault tolerance and is only about speed.

flashcards.back: A geographically distributed set of edge servers that cache content closer to end users, reducing the round-trip distance data has to travel and offloading traffic from the origin server.
flashcards.detail: A CDN mainly helps with latency and origin load, not raw available bandwidth, so before recommending one, check whether the scenario describes a latency problem (distance) or a bandwidth problem (capacity).

flashcards.back: A formal, documented process for proposing, reviewing, approving, and recording a change to production systems, including a rollback plan, before the change is actually made.
flashcards.detail: Once an approved change is completed, the CMDB (configuration management database) should be updated so that it always reflects the environment's true current state.

flashcards.back: A documented, step-by-step procedure for a specific operational task or incident response, written so it can be followed consistently by different people (or triggered automatically) with the same result each time.
flashcards.detail: A runbook is what automation and orchestration tooling actually executes — the runbook is the procedure, and the tooling carries it out without a human performing each step by hand.

flashcards.back: A periodic probe the load balancer sends to each backend instance to confirm it's actually able to serve traffic — an instance that fails enough consecutive checks is automatically taken out of rotation until it passes again.
flashcards.detail: This is what keeps a load balancing algorithm resilient to a failed instance — the algorithm only ever picks among instances the health check currently considers healthy.

flashcards.back: A cloud-delivered, centrally managed firewall service applied across an environment without deploying and maintaining physical or virtual firewall appliances at every location.
flashcards.detail: FWaaS commonly bundles stateful packet filtering and IDS/IPS-style inspection into one managed service, rather than stitching them together from separate appliances.

flashcards.back: A dedicated infrastructure layer (typically sidecar proxies alongside each service) that handles service-to-service traffic concerns — routing, retries, encryption, observability — without every microservice implementing that logic itself.
flashcards.detail: In a Kubernetes cluster, a service mesh's sidecar proxies are commonly injected into each pod, working alongside the application containers rather than replacing them.

flashcards.back: A Type 1 hypervisor runs directly on the physical hardware with no host OS underneath it — the standard for production datacenters and cloud providers. A Type 2 hypervisor runs as an application on top of a regular host OS, more common for a desktop/test environment.
flashcards.detail: Removing the host OS layer is exactly why Type 1 has less overhead and better performance — there is one less layer between the VM and the physical hardware than there is under a Type 2 hypervisor running on a regular desktop OS.

flashcards.back: Lets a user authenticate once and gain access to multiple independent systems without signing in separately to each one, using a shared trust relationship between the identity provider and each application.
flashcards.detail: SSO covers only the authentication piece of AAA — it doesn't decide what a user can do once signed in, only that they don't have to prove who they are over and over.

flashcards.back: A deployment approach where servers or containers are never modified after being provisioned — a change means replacing the instance entirely with a newly built one, rather than patching a live system in place.
flashcards.detail: This pairs naturally with Infrastructure as Code: if the whole environment is defined in code, replacing an instance instead of patching it becomes cheap and repeatable rather than risky.

flashcards.back: Deliberately injecting failures into a production or production-like system (killing an instance, adding latency, cutting a dependency) to verify that resilience mechanisms actually work as designed, instead of only assuming they do.
flashcards.detail: This is how a team validates its high availability, fault tolerance, and disaster recovery claims, rather than discovering the gaps for the first time during a real outage.

flashcards.back: An architecture that separates the control plane (the logic deciding how traffic should be routed) from the data plane (the hardware that just forwards packets), letting routing policy be managed centrally through software instead of configured device-by-device. A software-driven load balancer or a cloud-delivered firewall service is an everyday example of that same centralized, policy-driven control applied to one specific network function instead of the whole network.
flashcards.detail: SDN is the generalization; a single load balancer or a single FWaaS deployment is just one narrow application of the same control-plane/data-plane split across an entire network.

flashcards.back: A configuration switch that lets new code ship to production while hidden and turned off, with actually exposing it to users treated as a separate, later decision -- decoupling deployment from release. This pairs naturally with continuous deployment, since code can ship straight to production automatically without also being visible to anyone yet, and gives canary deployment-style control over exposure without needing a whole separate release process.
flashcards.detail: Deploying code and releasing it to users aren't the same event -- a feature flag is exactly what lets a team tell those two moments apart.

flashcards.back: A security appliance placed in front of a web application that inspects HTTP request content specifically for application-layer attacks like SQL injection and cross-site scripting, unlike a traditional network firewall filtering only by port and IP address. A WAF is often layered alongside network-level IDS/IPS inspection, but works one level up the stack -- reading the actual HTTP payload rather than just packet headers.
flashcards.detail: A WAF blind to encrypted payloads is a common gap -- it typically needs to sit where TLS is already terminated, or hold the private key itself, to actually inspect the request content it's meant to protect.

flashcards.back: Dedicated, tamper-resistant hardware that generates, stores, and performs operations with cryptographic keys internally, so the raw key material is never exposed to the operating system or application memory. An HSM frequently backs a Certificate Authority's private key in a PKI deployment, and is also commonly used to protect the keys behind disk, database, and application encryption.
flashcards.detail: Losing access to an HSM (a failed device with no backup key ceremony performed) can be as damaging as a breach -- the keys inside are deliberately built to never be extracted, which cuts both ways.

flashcards.back: In an active-active cluster, every node handles traffic at the same time, sharing the load across all of them. In an active-passive cluster, one or more standby nodes sit idle and only take over once the active node fails. Active-active makes fuller use of available hardware; active-passive is simpler to keep consistent, since only one node is ever accepting writes.
flashcards.detail: Active-active and active-passive are both ways of achieving high availability -- the choice decides how fast failover happens and how much of the cluster's capacity sits idle waiting for a failure.

flashcards.back: N+1 redundancy provisions one spare unit beyond what current load requires, so a single failure can be absorbed without a service impact. N+2 provisions two spares, tolerating two simultaneous failures (or one failure plus planned maintenance on another unit) at a higher ongoing cost.
flashcards.detail: This is the same raise-the-cost-for-more-resilience trade-off as choosing between hot, warm, and cold DR sites -- more spare capacity costs more every day it isn't needed, in exchange for surviving a worse day.

flashcards.front: Kubernetes: Deployment, ReplicaSet, and Service objects
flashcards.back: A ReplicaSet keeps a specified number of identical pod replicas running, replacing any that fail. A Deployment manages ReplicaSets on your behalf, handling rolling updates and rollbacks as the desired pod spec changes. A Service gives a stable network address and DNS name that routes to whichever healthy pods currently exist, even as individual pods are replaced underneath it.
flashcards.detail: Building on pods, nodes, and clusters -- a Service solves exactly the problem individual pods have: pods come and go with new IPs each time, but the Service address stays constant so nothing else has to track that churn.

flashcards.back: A network segment that sits between an untrusted network (the internet) and the trusted internal network, holding public-facing servers like web or mail servers behind their own firewall. A second firewall separates the DMZ from the internal network, so a compromise of a DMZ host doesn't automatically reach internal systems.
flashcards.detail: A DMZ is network segmentation applied at the perimeter specifically -- it limits how far a breach of an internet-facing server can spread, the same blast-radius goal behind Zero Trust, just enforced with topology instead of per-request verification.

flashcards.back: Granting a user or service account only the minimum access needed to perform its required task, and nothing more. It limits what a mistake, a compromised credential, or a misused role can actually reach.
flashcards.detail: Least privilege is what both RBAC and ABAC are supposed to enforce in practice -- assigning a role or attribute set that's broader than the job actually requires defeats the point of either access control model.

flashcards.back: A security group is a stateful firewall applied at the instance/interface level -- allow a request in, and its response is automatically allowed back out. A network ACL (NACL) is a stateless filter applied at the subnet level, evaluating inbound and outbound traffic independently, so both directions need their own explicit rule.
flashcards.detail: This is the stateful-versus-stateless distinction applied to two specific, commonly paired cloud controls -- a NACL sets a broad subnet-wide boundary, while security groups add finer, per-instance rules inside it.

flashcards.front: The "6 R's" of cloud migration strategy
flashcards.back: Rehost (move as-is, "lift and shift"), Replatform (move with light optimization, no architecture change), Repurchase (switch to a different, often SaaS, product), Refactor/Re-architect (redesign for cloud-native services), Retire (decommission, since it's no longer needed), and Retain (keep it on-premises for now).
flashcards.detail: Rehost lines up with the lift-and-shift style of P2C and V2C migration, moving a workload largely as-is; Refactor is the opposite end of that same spectrum, redesigning around cloud-native services instead of just relocating the existing build.

flashcards.front: Functional, regression, performance, and usability testing
flashcards.back: Functional testing checks that a feature works as specified. Regression testing confirms a change didn't break something that previously worked. Performance (load) testing measures behavior under expected or peak traffic. Usability testing evaluates how easily real users can actually use the result.
flashcards.detail: A CI/CD pipeline leans hardest on automated functional and regression testing -- usability testing in particular usually still needs a human, which is part of why continuous deployment is riskier without it.

flashcards.front: Dev, test, staging, and production environments
flashcards.back: Development is where code is actively written and experimented on. Test (QA) runs automated and manual tests against a build in isolation. Staging mirrors production as closely as possible, for final verification before release. Production is the live environment actual users depend on.
flashcards.detail: A blue-green or canary deployment moves a release from staging into production -- staging is meant to catch what dev and test alone would miss, by matching production's configuration as closely as possible first.

flashcards.front: Reserved vs. on-demand vs. spot instances
flashcards.back: On-demand instances are paid for by usage with no commitment, at the highest per-hour rate. Reserved instances commit to a term (often 1-3 years) in exchange for a substantially lower rate, suited to steady, predictable workloads. Spot instances use the provider's unused capacity at the deepest discount, but can be reclaimed by the provider with little notice -- a fit only for fault-tolerant, interruptible work.
flashcards.detail: Choosing wrong here is a common capacity planning mistake -- reserving capacity for a bursty, unpredictable workload wastes the commitment, while running a steady production database on spot instances risks losing it mid-transaction.

flashcards.back: MTTR (Mean Time To Repair/Recovery) is the average time it takes to fix a failure and restore service once it occurs. MTBF (Mean Time Between Failures) is the average time a system runs between failures -- a measure of reliability rather than recovery speed.
flashcards.detail: MTBF is about how often something breaks; MTTR is about how fast it gets fixed once it does -- a system can fail often (short MTBF) and still keep good uptime if its MTTR is low enough. Both are measured historical averages, unlike an SLA's negotiated targets.

flashcards.back: Attaching key-value metadata (like department, environment, or cost center) to cloud resources at creation, so they can be filtered, grouped, and attributed automatically instead of tracked by memory or naming convention alone.
flashcards.detail: Tagging is what makes chargeback, showback, and a CMDB practical at scale -- without a consistent tag on every resource, there's no reliable way to automatically attribute cost or ownership to the right team.

flashcards.back: A hypervisor technique for reclaiming memory from a VM that isn't actively using all of what it was allocated, by asking a driver inside the guest to artificially claim ("balloon") that memory so the hypervisor can hand it to another VM that needs it more. Pushed too far, the guest starts swapping to disk instead, which is far slower than RAM.
flashcards.detail: Ballooning shows up alongside CPU ready time as one of the hypervisor-level metrics used to investigate a noisy-neighbor problem -- a VM whose own metrics look fine can still be starved if the host is aggressively ballooning its memory for another tenant.

flashcards.back: A top-down approach starts at the layer closest to the user (the application) and works downward through the web server, database, and network, narrowing down where a delay or failure is actually introduced. A bottom-up approach starts at the opposite end, checking physical connectivity and the network first before moving up toward the application.
flashcards.detail: Neither approach is universally correct -- the better starting point usually depends on which layer the reported symptom most directly points to, rather than always defaulting to the same end of the stack.

flashcards.back: Quorum requires a cluster to have a majority of voting members able to communicate before it will act as the primary, preventing a split group from both claiming to be in charge. Fencing goes further, actively isolating or powering off a node that's lost quorum, so it can't keep accepting writes even if it still believes it's the primary.
flashcards.detail: Quorum and fencing are the standard defenses against a split-brain condition -- without them, a network partition can leave two nodes both acting as primary at once, each accepting writes the other doesn't know about.

flashcards.back: Burstable instance types earn CPU credits during periods of low usage and spend them during bursts of higher CPU demand. Once the credit balance is exhausted, the instance is throttled to a fixed baseline performance level until it earns more credits, even though its own workload and configuration haven't changed.
flashcards.detail: This produces a sluggish-VM symptom that looks a lot like a noisy-neighbor problem at first glance, but checking the instance's own CPU credit balance -- not another tenant's activity on the host -- is what actually tells the two apart.

flashcards.back: A surge of near-simultaneous requests -- often triggered when a cache expires, a service recovers from an outage, or many clients retry at the same moment -- overwhelms a backend that could easily handle that same total request volume if it were spread out over time.
flashcards.detail: A common trigger is every client using the exact same retry interval after a failure; staggering retries with jitter (a small random delay) is the standard fix, spreading the reconnection surge out instead of letting it all land in the same instant.

flashcards.back: A condition where an autoscaling group repeatedly scales out and then back in within a short period because the scaling thresholds sit too close to normal, everyday load -- ordinary variation keeps crossing the trigger in both directions.
flashcards.detail: The fix mirrors baseline-versus-threshold discipline applied to autoscaling instead of alerting: widen the margin between the scale-out and scale-in triggers, or add a cooldown period, so routine fluctuation stops re-triggering a scaling action every few minutes.

flashcards.front: Core network troubleshooting tools: ping, traceroute, and packet capture
flashcards.back: Ping tests basic reachability and round-trip latency to a host. Traceroute (tracert) maps the hop-by-hop path a packet takes, showing where along that path delay or loss is actually introduced. A packet capture (e.g., tcpdump, Wireshark) records the raw traffic itself for deep inspection, for when the first two tools aren't specific enough to explain the symptom.
flashcards.detail: These three escalate in effort on purpose: ping confirms there's a problem, traceroute narrows down roughly where it is, and a packet capture is for when you need to see exactly what was actually sent and received.

flashcards.front: API throttling vs. service quota limit
flashcards.back: Throttling is a temporary rate limit -- the same request would succeed if it were sent more slowly, and it typically returns an HTTP 429. A service quota limit is a hard ceiling on a resource count (such as VMs allowed per region) that a request fails against no matter how slowly it's sent, until the quota itself is raised.
flashcards.detail: Throttling calls for backing off and retrying; a quota limit calls for requesting a limit increase from the provider -- retrying the exact same request against a quota failure just reproduces the same failure again.

flashcards.back: A condition where traffic from host A to host B takes one network path, but the return traffic from B back to A takes a different path -- often breaking a stateful device, like a firewall or a NAT gateway, sitting on only one of the two paths and never seeing the matching half of the connection.
flashcards.detail: This builds on stateful packet filtering: a stateful firewall only recognizes return traffic that matches a connection it saw leave, so when that return traffic arrives over a different path, the firewall has no record of it at all.

flashcards.back: A container that repeatedly fails shortly after starting, gets automatically restarted by the orchestrator, fails again, and repeats -- usually caused by a bad configuration, a missing dependency, or an application error that happens on every single startup rather than only sometimes.
flashcards.detail: Because the orchestrator in a Kubernetes cluster keeps restarting it automatically, a crash loop can look like a series of short outages in a monitoring dashboard rather than one persistent failure -- checking the container's own startup logs, not just its up/down status, is what actually reveals the real cause.

flashcards.back: Aggregating logs from many separate systems -- application, web server, database, network -- into one searchable platform, so events across all of them can be lined up by timestamp to reconstruct what actually happened during an incident.
flashcards.detail: Without correlation, each system's logs only tell part of the story; this is the same aggregation step that a SIEM builds on, turning scattered log entries into one coherent timeline an analyst (or an automated response) can act on.

flashcards.back: A condition where on-call staff receive so many low-value or noisy alerts that they start ignoring or delaying their response to all of them, including the real ones. Tuning -- adding a sustained-duration condition, adjusting thresholds, or suppressing a known-noisy check -- reduces volume without losing genuine signal.
flashcards.detail: This is the practical cost of skipping baselining before setting thresholds -- a threshold set without a solid baseline tends to misfire constantly, and alert fatigue is what that misfiring costs a team over time.

flashcards.back: A defined period -- commonly around a major event like a holiday shopping peak or a scheduled audit -- during which no non-emergency changes are permitted, to minimize the risk of a self-inflicted outage at the worst possible time.
flashcards.detail: A change freeze doesn't replace the change management process; it temporarily tightens it -- an emergency change made during a freeze still has to go through added scrutiny and get documented, rather than skipping the process altogether.

flashcards.back: A structured review held after an incident is resolved, focused on identifying contributing factors and process gaps rather than assigning individual blame, so people report what actually happened honestly instead of covering up a mistake out of fear.
flashcards.detail: This is where root cause analysis (as opposed to a quick workaround) formally gets written down and assigned an owner -- without a scheduled review like this, a root cause investigation started under time pressure is easy to never actually finish.

flashcards.back: A predefined, tested procedure for reverting to the last known-good version if a new release fails verification, prepared before the release goes out rather than improvised after something has already broken.
flashcards.detail: Blue-green and canary deployments already offer an easy rollback path by design -- switching traffic back, or pulling the canary slice -- but a rolling or in-place deployment needs this plan spelled out explicitly, since reverting isn't automatic the way it is with a full duplicate environment.

flashcards.back: Failover is switching production operation over to a disaster recovery site after the primary site fails. Failback is the separate, later step of returning operation to the primary site once it's restored and verified healthy -- and it carries its own risk of data loss or conflict if changes made at the DR site during failover aren't properly reconciled first.
flashcards.detail: Testing a DR plan built on hot, warm, or cold sites often only rehearses the failover half; a DR test that skips failback can leave a team discovering failback's reconciliation problems for the first time during a real event.

flashcards.back: A SIEM (Security Information and Event Management) platform ingests and correlates logs and alerts from many systems into a single view for an analyst to investigate. A SOAR (Security Orchestration, Automation, and Response) platform goes further, triggering automated response actions -- like isolating a host or disabling an account -- based on what the SIEM detects, without waiting for a person to act first.
flashcards.detail: SIEM and SOAR pair up the same way an IDS and an IPS do -- one observes and correlates, the other acts -- and in practice a SIEM commonly feeds the alerts that a SOAR platform then automates a response to.

flashcards.back: Periodically replacing passwords, API keys, and certificates with new ones on a defined schedule (or immediately after a suspected compromise), so a credential that leaked or was exposed has only a limited window in which it's actually still valid.
flashcards.detail: This limits the damage of a leaked secret the same way the principle of least privilege limits the damage of an over-broad grant -- neither one assumes a breach won't happen, both just shrink what it can actually reach, or how long it stays useful, once one does.

flashcards.back: Security and operations duties are split between the cloud provider and the customer. The provider secures the underlying infrastructure (facilities, hardware, hypervisor), while the customer secures what they put on it: their data, identities, access settings, and, depending on the service model, the guest OS and applications.
flashcards.detail: The line moves with the service model: in IaaS the customer patches the guest OS, in SaaS the provider does. Data and access management always stay with the customer.

flashcards.back: A VPC (called a virtual network in some clouds) is a logically isolated private network inside a public cloud, defined by an IP range in CIDR notation. It is divided into subnets, commonly public ones with a route to an internet gateway and private ones without, and subnets are placed in availability zones.
flashcards.detail: In a typical three-tier design, web servers sit in a public subnet while application and database servers sit in private subnets with no direct internet route.

flashcards.back: Peering connects two networks directly so they can talk privately, but it is not transitive. A transit gateway is a central hub that many VPCs and on-premises networks attach to, letting them route to each other without building a full mesh of peering links.
flashcards.detail: Ten VPCs in a full peering mesh need 45 connections, while a transit gateway needs only 10 attachments, which is why it scales better for many networks.

flashcards.back: A site-to-site VPN sends encrypted traffic over the public internet, so it is quick and inexpensive to set up but its latency and bandwidth vary. A dedicated connection is a private link from the datacenter to the provider, with consistent latency and higher bandwidth, but at higher cost and longer lead time, and it is not encrypted by default.
flashcards.detail: A common pattern is a dedicated connection as the primary path with a VPN as an encrypted backup. Choose the dedicated link when a scenario stresses predictable latency or high throughput.

flashcards.front: Serverless computing and Function as a service (FaaS)
flashcards.back: Serverless means the provider runs and scales the servers while the customer pays per execution. FaaS is its event-triggered form: small functions run in response to events such as an HTTP request or a file upload, and scale down to zero when idle.
flashcards.detail: It suits spiky, event-driven work. Typical trade-offs are execution time limits, cold-start delay on first invocation, and tighter lock-in to the provider's event services.

flashcards.back: A monolith packages all of an application's functions into one deployable unit. Microservices split it into small, loosely coupled services that communicate through APIs, so each can be deployed, scaled, and fail independently of the others.
flashcards.detail: Microservices let you scale only a busy checkout service, but they add network calls and make troubleshooting harder, which is why tracing and centralized logging become important.

flashcards.back: A region is a geographic area containing multiple datacenters. An availability zone is one or more isolated datacenters inside a region, with independent power, cooling, and networking. Spreading across zones protects against a datacenter failure, and spreading across regions protects against a regional disaster.
flashcards.detail: High availability within a region points to a multi-zone design, while disaster recovery or data locality requirements point to a second region.

flashcards.back: Relational databases store data in tables with a fixed schema, use SQL, and provide ACID transactions, which suits structured, related data. Non-relational databases, such as key-value, document, column, and graph stores, use flexible schemas and usually scale out horizontally.
flashcards.detail: Orders and payments that need strict consistency fit a relational database, while session data or a huge product catalog with varied fields fits a key-value or document store.

flashcards.back: Controls that detect and block sensitive data, such as card numbers or personal records, from leaving approved boundaries through email, uploads, endpoints, or cloud storage. DLP inspects content and applies rules based on how the data is classified.
flashcards.detail: A scenario about stopping staff from uploading customer records to personal storage points to DLP. It works best after data has been classified.

flashcards.back: Data sovereignty is the legal principle that data is subject to the laws of the jurisdiction where it is collected, stored, or processed. Data locality is the physical or geographic location where the data is stored and processed.
flashcards.detail: Choosing an in-country region satisfies a locality rule, but backups or replicas copied to another region can break it, so check replication and backup settings too.

flashcards.back: Federation lets one identity provider authenticate users for services run by other organizations or apps, so users sign in once with their home credentials. SAML passes signed XML assertions and is common for enterprise web single sign-on, while OpenID Connect adds an identity layer on OAuth 2.0 using JSON tokens, common for modern web and mobile apps.
flashcards.detail: A requirement for partner staff to use their own company logins without separate accounts in your cloud is a federation scenario.

flashcards.back: Storing and distributing credentials such as API keys, passwords, tokens, and certificates in a dedicated vault service with access control, audit logging, and rotation, instead of hardcoding them in source code, images, or configuration files.
flashcards.detail: A cloud key found in a public Git repository is the failure it prevents. Applications fetch secrets at runtime using their own identity, which pairs with credential rotation.

flashcards.back: A hardened, closely monitored host that is the single entry point for administrative SSH or RDP access into private instances, which have no public IP addresses. Admins connect to the bastion first and then onward to the target.
flashcards.detail: It shrinks the exposed attack surface to one logged system instead of many. Managed bastion services provide the same pattern without maintaining the host yourself.

flashcards.back: Vulnerability scanning automatically checks systems, images, and containers for known weaknesses. Findings are usually identified by CVE (Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures) numbers and ranked by severity so teams can prioritize patching or configuration fixes.
flashcards.detail: A scan only finds problems, so remediation and a re-scan to verify the fix must follow. It differs from a penetration test, which actively tries to exploit weaknesses.

flashcards.back: Layering several independent security controls, such as network segmentation, firewalls, identity controls, encryption, and monitoring, so that the failure or bypass of any one layer does not expose the asset.
flashcards.detail: A WAF in front of an app is one layer, but the app should still validate input, the database should restrict access, and data should be encrypted. Relying on a single control is the exam trap.

flashcards.front: Compliance frameworks: PCI DSS, ISO 27001, and SOC 2
flashcards.back: PCI DSS sets requirements for protecting payment card data. ISO/IEC 27001 specifies an information security management system that can be independently certified. SOC 2 is an audit report on a service organization's controls against trust criteria such as security and availability.
flashcards.detail: A provider's SOC 2 report or ISO certificate is evidence about its own controls, but it does not make the customer's workload compliant. That still depends on the shared responsibility model.

flashcards.back: Symmetric encryption uses one shared secret key to both encrypt and decrypt, and it is fast, so it protects bulk data. Asymmetric encryption uses a public and private key pair, is slower, and is used for key exchange, digital signatures, and certificates.
flashcards.detail: TLS combines them: asymmetric cryptography authenticates the server and agrees on a key, then symmetric encryption protects the actual session data.

flashcards.back: The gradual divergence of a deployed environment from its intended, defined configuration, usually caused by manual changes made outside the automation. Drift detection compares the actual state with the declared infrastructure-as-code state and flags the differences.
flashcards.detail: A server hand-edited during an outage is the classic cause. Reapplying the IaC definition, or replacing the instance, brings it back to the declared state.

flashcards.back: Declarative tools, such as Terraform or cloud templates, describe the desired end state and the tool works out the steps. Imperative scripts, such as shell or CLI commands, specify each step in order, so the author handles ordering and existing state.
flashcards.detail: Running a declarative definition twice leaves the same result, while a naive imperative script may create duplicates the second time. That repeatability is the exam point.

flashcards.back: A pre-built, hardened, tested virtual machine or container image containing the OS, patches, agents, and baseline configuration, used as the standard template for launching new instances so every instance starts identical.
flashcards.detail: Patching means building a new golden image and replacing instances from it. That reduces boot-time setup and configuration drift.

flashcards.front: Source control: branching, pull requests, and merging
flashcards.back: Version control, commonly Git, records every change to code and IaC. Teams make changes on separate branches, then open a pull request to merge into the main branch, which triggers code review and automated checks before the merge.
flashcards.detail: Protecting the main branch so changes need an approved pull request keeps unreviewed infrastructure changes out of production.

flashcards.back: An artifact is the versioned output of a build stage, such as a container image, VM image, or package (RPM, Debian, ZIP, tar). It is stored in a repository or registry and promoted unchanged through test, staging, and production.
flashcards.detail: Build once and deploy that same artifact everywhere. Rebuilding separately for each environment risks differences that only show up in production.

flashcards.back: Two text formats used for IaC templates and configuration files. JSON uses braces and quoted keys and is strict, with no comments. YAML uses indentation, is more readable, and allows comments. Both can express variables, lists, and nested structures.
flashcards.detail: A YAML pipeline that fails to parse is often an indentation error, while a JSON file fails on a stray trailing comma.

flashcards.back: Automation that runs in response to an event rather than a schedule or a person, such as a file arriving in storage, an alert firing, or a code push. It is commonly built with webhooks, message queues, and serverless functions.
flashcards.detail: An alert that triggers a function to restart a failed service is event-driven. A nightly script is scheduled, not event-driven.

flashcards.back: The ability to understand a system's internal state from the data it emits. Logs are records of discrete events, metrics are numeric measurements over time such as CPU or latency, and traces follow one request across services.
flashcards.detail: Metrics show that latency rose, traces show which service in the chain is slow, and logs show the error behind it. Together they explain why, not just that something is wrong.

flashcards.back: Follows a single request as it passes through multiple services, assigning it a trace ID and recording a timed span for each hop, so you can see where time is spent or where an error originates.
flashcards.detail: It is the right tool when a request is slow only sometimes in a microservices app. Separate per-service logs cannot easily be lined up to show the path of one request.

flashcards.back: Triggered (dynamic) scaling adds or removes capacity when a metric crosses a threshold. Scheduled scaling changes capacity at set times for predictable demand. Manual scaling is an operator changing capacity directly.
flashcards.detail: A known 9 a.m. rush calls for scheduled scaling, while an unpredictable traffic spike calls for triggered scaling.

flashcards.back: A retention policy sets how long backups are kept before deletion, driven by recovery needs and compliance. Replication copies backups to another zone, region, or account so that a site failure does not destroy both the data and its backups. Backups should also be encrypted.
flashcards.detail: Backups stored beside the primary data will not survive a regional outage. The 3-2-1 rule means three copies, on two media types, with one kept offsite.

flashcards.front: Recovery testing: in-place vs. parallel recovery
flashcards.back: Restoring from backup on a schedule proves the backups work. In-place recovery restores over the original resource, replacing its current state. Parallel recovery restores to a separate new resource, leaving the original untouched so the data can be checked before cutover.
flashcards.detail: A backup that has never been test-restored is unproven. Parallel recovery is safer for tests because production is not overwritten.

flashcards.back: Ephemeral data disappears when an instance stops or is replaced, such as instance store disks, container filesystems, and memory. Persistent data survives, kept on durable volumes, databases, or object storage.
flashcards.detail: Autoscaled instances that are destroyed on scale-in lose any logs or files stored locally, so those should be shipped to central persistent storage.

flashcards.back: Tracking cloud resources from provisioning through use, updates, and retirement. Proper decommissioning removes access, securely deletes data, deletes dependent items such as disks, snapshots, and IP addresses, and updates the CMDB.
flashcards.detail: Skipping it leaves orphaned resources that cost money and leftover data that is a security risk.

flashcards.back: Matching an instance's size (vCPU, memory, storage) to the workload actually observed in monitoring data, so you neither pay for idle capacity nor run into limits. It often reduces cost without hurting performance.
flashcards.detail: A VM averaging 8 percent CPU is a candidate to downsize. This is separate from buying reserved capacity, which changes the price, not the size.

flashcards.back: The maximum transmission unit is the largest packet a link can carry. A mismatch, often caused by VPN or tunnel overhead, makes large packets fragment or be dropped, especially when the don't-fragment flag is set and the ICMP messages that report the problem are blocked.
flashcards.detail: The classic symptom is that ping and the TCP handshake work but large transfers or HTTPS pages hang. Lowering the MTU or clamping the TCP segment size on the tunnel fixes it.

flashcards.back: On a virtualized host, the time a VM has work ready to run but waits for the hypervisor to schedule it on a physical CPU. High CPU ready time means vCPUs are contending for cores, even when utilization inside the guest looks low.
flashcards.detail: A sluggish VM with low guest CPU but high CPU ready points to host contention. Fixes include reducing overcommitment, right-sizing vCPU counts, or moving VMs, as with a noisy neighbor.

flashcards.front: Time synchronization failure (NTP and clock skew)
flashcards.back: Systems use NTP (Network Time Protocol) to keep clocks aligned. Clock skew breaks anything that depends on timestamps, including Kerberos authentication, TLS certificate validity checks, token expiry, and log correlation.
flashcards.detail: Sudden authentication failures on one VM, with a healthy network and valid credentials, point to its clock. Kerberos tolerates only a few minutes of skew, five by default.

flashcards.back: A record's time to live is how long resolvers may cache its answer. After a record changes, clients keep using the old answer until the TTL expires, so a cutover appears to work for some users and not others.
flashcards.detail: Lower the TTL ahead of a planned migration or blue-green switch so the change takes effect quickly. Flushing a local cache fixes only that machine.

flashcards.back: Packet loss is the share of packets that never arrive, forcing retransmission in TCP or causing gaps in UDP traffic. Jitter is variation in packet delay. Both hurt real-time traffic such as voice and video more than file transfers.
flashcards.detail: Choppy voice calls with a healthy bandwidth test point to loss or jitter, not capacity. Check path statistics with tools like ping or mtr and review QoS settings.

flashcards.back: A software bug in which memory is allocated but never released, so usage climbs over time until the process or host slows, swaps heavily, or is killed for running out of memory.
flashcards.detail: A steady upward memory trend that a restart temporarily clears is the tell. Moving to a larger instance only delays the failure, so the fix is in the application.

questions.question: Four regional credit unions want to split the cost of one cloud platform built to satisfy the same regulator-mandated audit controls. A single provider operates it, and only the four member institutions may use it. Which deployment model does this describe?
options: Community cloud, shared by organizations with common compliance needs
Hybrid cloud, because the provider connects several separate tenants
Private cloud, because access is limited to a defined set of customers
Multi-cloud, because several organizations contribute to the platform
questions.explanation: Community cloud is infrastructure shared by a small group of organizations with a common concern, here the same regulatory controls, and closed to the general public. Private cloud is dedicated to a single organization, so restricting access to a list of customers does not make it private. Hybrid means private and public environments connected together, which is not described. Multi-cloud means using more than one provider, but this platform has only one provider.

questions.question: An application automatically adds server instances at 9 AM on weekdays and removes them at 6 PM, based on a fixed calendar schedule rather than real-time load. Which description is most accurate?
options: Vertical scaling, because capacity changes at fixed times every day
Fault tolerance, since the system keeps running without any interruption during the schedule change
Elasticity, since it happens without manual intervention
Scheduled scaling, a form of scalability but not elasticity
questions.explanation: This is automatic, but it is reacting to a calendar, not to real-time demand. Elasticity specifically means capacity that follows actual, current load. It also adds whole instances (horizontal), not a bigger existing one (vertical), and it has nothing to do with tolerating failures.
questions.whyTested: This one stacks four scaling/resilience terms against a single scenario specifically to catch the common shortcut of equating 'automatic' with 'elastic' — the exam wants you to notice that a fixed calendar schedule isn't reacting to real-time demand at all. It's a favorite trap shape because scheduled autoscaling and true elasticity look identical from the outside; only checking what's actually triggering the change tells them apart.

questions.question: A single-instance licensed database is running out of memory. The vendor's license does not support clustering and the team has no time to re-architect, so they move the VM to a larger instance size. Which trade-off must they accept?
options: Each additional instance must hold its own copy of the data, which can drift out of sync
It will likely need a restart, and it can only grow to the largest size offered
A load balancer becomes a single point of failure for all database connections
Capacity follows demand automatically, but only up to the autoscaling group's maximum
questions.explanation: Resizing one instance is vertical scaling (scaling up). It usually needs a restart to apply and it hits a ceiling at the biggest instance size available. The other options describe consequences of horizontal scaling or autoscaling, which this team is not doing: replicas holding separate copies of data, a load balancer in front of the database, and elastic capacity bounded by a group maximum.

questions.question: A database has an RPO of 15 minutes and an RTO of 4 hours. Transaction logs currently ship to the DR site hourly, and a rehearsed failover takes about 2 hours. Which single change brings the design into compliance?
options: Automate failover so that it completes in under 15 minutes
Extend backup retention at the DR site from 7 to 30 days
Ship transaction logs to the DR site at least every 15 minutes
Add a second warm standby in a different region
questions.explanation: The gap is data loss: hourly shipping can lose up to 60 minutes of transactions, which breaks a 15-minute RPO, so the shipping interval must shrink. The 2-hour failover already fits inside the 4-hour RTO, so speeding it up fixes nothing that is broken. Longer retention changes how far back you can restore, not how recent the newest copy is, and a second standby adds redundancy without changing the log-shipping interval.

questions.question: A media company must retain several petabytes of finished video for seven years at the lowest cost. Files are written once, retrieved whole by a web application through HTTP API calls, and never edited in place. No application needs a mounted drive. Which storage type fits best?
options: Object storage with lifecycle rules that move older files to cheaper tiers
Block storage volumes attached to a fleet of VMs, with snapshots
Instance-local ephemeral disks replicated across several hosts
File storage exposed to the application servers over SMB shares
questions.explanation: Write-once, whole-file retrieval over HTTP at petabyte scale is the object storage use case, and lifecycle rules help control long-term cost. File storage adds a hierarchical, mountable filesystem that nothing here needs. Block storage is for low-latency random I/O such as a database disk. Ephemeral instance disks are lost when the instance stops, which is unacceptable for a seven-year retention requirement.

questions.question: An application team wants one public address that sends requests for /api to a pool of API servers and requests for /images to a separate pool of media servers. Which load balancer approach can make that decision?
options: A Layer 4 load balancer using the least-connections algorithm
A Layer 4 load balancer with source-IP affinity enabled
A Layer 7 (application-layer) load balancer that inspects HTTP request paths
DNS round robin returning each pool's addresses in rotation
questions.explanation: Routing by URL path requires reading the HTTP request, which only a Layer 7 load balancer does. A Layer 4 balancer sees IP addresses and ports, so algorithms such as least connections or source-IP affinity only choose among servers in one pool and cannot tell /api from /images. DNS round robin hands out addresses in rotation before any request exists, so it has no visibility into the path at all.

questions.question: Customers in Southeast Asia report slow page loads for static images served from a single origin in Europe. The origin's network link averages 15% utilization and its CPU is low. Which change most directly addresses the complaint?
options: Upgrade the origin's network link to a higher bandwidth tier
Scale the origin vertically to a larger instance size
Add read replicas of the origin's database in the same region
Cache the static content at edge locations near those users with a CDN
questions.explanation: Low link utilization and low CPU rule out a capacity problem, so the delay is distance: every request crosses the globe. A CDN caches content at edge locations close to users, cutting round-trip latency and offloading the origin. More bandwidth does not shorten the round trip, a bigger instance is not the bottleneck, and database replicas in the same region do nothing for static files served to distant users.

questions.question: After a breach, investigators confirm the attacker logged in with a valid stolen password and that the compromised role legitimately allowed the deletions. They cannot tell which records were deleted or when, because audit logging was disabled on the system. Which AAA function was missing?
options: Authentication, which verifies the identity presenting credentials
Accounting, which records what each identity actually did
Authorization, which limits what a verified identity may do
Federation, which lets one identity provider vouch for users across systems
questions.explanation: Accounting is the logging of what was actually done, and its absence is why the investigators cannot reconstruct the deletions. Authentication did its job in the narrow sense, since the credential was valid, and authorization did too, since the role permitted the actions. Federation is a way of sharing identities between systems and has no bearing on producing an audit trail.

questions.question: A cloud team must let contractors reach only resources tagged with their own project, only during contract hours, and only from managed devices. New projects must not require creating new roles. Which access control model fits best?
options: ABAC, evaluating user, resource, and context attributes at request time
MAC, with system-assigned classification labels on every resource
RBAC, with a distinct role created for each project
DAC, with each resource owner granting access individually
questions.explanation: ABAC makes a decision per request from attributes such as the contractor's project, the resource's tag, the time, and device posture, so a new project needs only a new tag value, not a new role. RBAC would need a role per project and cannot express time or device conditions natively. MAC relies on centrally assigned classification labels, and DAC leaves grants to individual owners, which does not scale or enforce these contextual rules.

questions.question: A database volume is fully encrypted on disk, yet an attacker intercepted query results as they traveled from the database server to a reporting application over an internal network. Which control would most directly have prevented the interception?
options: Rotating the disk-encryption key more frequently
Requiring MFA for database administrator logins
Enabling transparent encryption on the reporting application's local cache
Enforcing TLS between the reporting application and the database
questions.explanation: The data was intercepted while moving across the network, so the missing control is encryption in transit, such as TLS on the database connection. Disk encryption was already in place and protects only stored data, so rotating its key does nothing for traffic on the wire. MFA governs who can log in, and encrypting the application's cache protects another at-rest copy, not the connection.
questions.whyTested: Cloud+ tests this pairing constantly because 'the database is encrypted' sounds like a complete answer even when the actual incident happened somewhere at-rest encryption was never involved — the exam wants you to track which specific state the data was in when the gap occurred. The distractors are all real, sensible controls that simply protect a different state or a different threat.

questions.question: A team wants to detect network attacks but guarantee that the detection tool can never interrupt production traffic, even on a false positive. Which deployment meets that requirement?
options: An inline IPS configured to drop packets that match attack signatures
A passive IDS fed a copy of traffic from a network tap or mirror port
A WAF in blocking mode placed in front of the web servers
An inline IPS configured to fail closed if its inspection engine stops
questions.explanation: A passive IDS only sees a copy of the traffic and raises alerts, so a false positive produces a noisy alert rather than an outage. An inline IPS sits in the traffic path and acts on matches, so a false positive drops legitimate packets, and failing closed makes an engine fault block traffic too. A WAF in blocking mode is likewise inline and can reject legitimate requests.

questions.question: An engineer adds an inbound allow rule for TCP 443 to a subnet-level filter. The web servers are healthy and their instance-level firewalls allow the traffic, yet clients still time out. The subnet filter evaluates each packet independently. What is most likely missing?
options: An IPS policy that explicitly trusts the clients' source addresses
A connection-tracking table large enough to hold all active sessions
An outbound rule on the subnet filter permitting the servers' reply traffic
A signature update so the filter recognizes HTTPS traffic
questions.explanation: A filter that evaluates every packet independently is stateless, so it does not recognize replies as belonging to an allowed connection; the response leaving the subnet needs its own outbound rule. A stateless filter keeps no connection table, so table size is irrelevant, and it uses simple rules rather than signatures or IPS trust policies.

questions.question: A payment processor wants application servers to hold no recoverable form of stored card numbers, yet customer service must still be able to retrieve the original number for a refund through a controlled lookup. Which technique fits?
options: Tokenization, with the real numbers held in a separate secured vault
Salted hashing of each card number before it is stored
Masking all but the last four digits when the number is stored
Symmetric encryption, with the key stored on the application server
questions.explanation: Tokenization stores a meaningless substitute on the application side and keeps the real number only in a separate vault, so the original can be retrieved through a controlled lookup but cannot be computed from the token. Encryption with a locally stored key leaves a recoverable form on the same server. Hashing is one-way, so the number could never be retrieved for a refund, and masking discards the digits it hides.

questions.question: After an attacker used a stolen VPN credential to join the internal network, an organization adopts Zero Trust. Which outcome would Zero Trust most directly have prevented?
options: The credential being phished from the user in the first place
The VPN requiring authentication at connect time
Reaching sensitive systems on the strength of network access alone
Any need to log or audit the attacker's later activity
questions.explanation: Zero Trust never grants trust based on network location, so being inside the network is not enough: each request to a sensitive system is verified on its own. It does not stop credential theft itself, it adds verification rather than removing it, and it increases rather than eliminates the need for logging and auditing.

questions.question: A release changes an API contract, so the old and new versions should not serve users side by side. The business wants a rollback measured in seconds and will fund a temporary duplicate of production. Which deployment strategy fits?
options: Canary deployment, shifting a small percentage of traffic to the new version first
Rolling deployment, updating a few instances at a time behind the load balancer
In-place deployment, updating every server directly during a maintenance window
Blue-green deployment, switching all traffic to a fully verified duplicate environment
questions.explanation: Blue-green keeps two identical environments, verifies the idle one, and then switches all traffic at once, so users see one version or the other, and rollback is just switching back. Canary and rolling deployments deliberately run both versions together while the rollout progresses, which the API change forbids. An in-place update has neither a duplicate to fall back on nor a seconds-long rollback.

questions.question: A company runs a full backup every Sunday and a differential backup every other day of the week. If a failure happens on Thursday, which backups are needed to fully restore the data, and in what order?
options: Sunday's full backup, then every differential from Monday through Wednesday, in sequence
Sunday's full backup, then Thursday's differential backup
Only Wednesday's differential backup
Sunday's full backup, then Wednesday's differential backup
questions.explanation: A differential backup captures everything changed since the last FULL backup, so the most recent differential (Wednesday's) already contains all of Monday through Wednesday's changes on its own — only the full plus that single latest differential are needed. Needing to replay every differential in sequence is the restore pattern for incremental backups, not differential.
questions.whyTested: Differential-vs-incremental restore order is one of the most reliably confused pairs on this exam, so questions like this build a multi-day backup chain and ask which specific backups are needed rather than just asking to define the terms — it's testing whether you worked through the restore logic rather than just recognizing a vocabulary word. The wrong answer that lists every day in sequence is deliberately shaped like the correct incremental-restore process, banking on you not noticing the backup type had changed.

questions.question: Two years ago a physical server was converted to a VM on the company's on-premises hypervisor. The team now exports that VM image and imports it unchanged into a provider's public cloud compute service. Which migration type is this move?
options: P2C, because the workload originally ran on physical hardware
V2C, because the source was already virtualized on-premises
V2V, because the VM is moving to a different hypervisor
P2V, because the server is being converted into a virtual machine
questions.explanation: The migration type is set by the state of the source right now: a workload that is already a VM on-premises and is moving into the cloud is V2C.
